headings.title: Introduction to Body Cavities
headings.content: Body cavities are internal spaces within the human body that protect, separate, and support internal organs. These fluid-filled spaces act as physical buffers against sudden jolts and movements when walking, running, or working. The human body is broadly divided into two main cavities: the **dorsal cavity**, which encases the central nervous system, and the **ventral cavity**, which houses visceral organs. Understanding these anatomical divisions forms the foundation of physical assessment, helping healthcare professionals map pain, locate organ pathology, and communicate findings accurately across multidisciplinary teams in Nigerian clinical settings.

headings.title: Dorsal Body Cavity: Cranial and Spinal Regions
headings.content:
Located near the posterior surface of the body, the **dorsal body cavity** is a continuous, closed space divided into two tightly protected regions:

1. **Cranial cavity**: Formed by the skull bones, it encloses, cushions, and protects the brain.
2. **Vertebral (spinal) cavity**: Formed by the vertebrae of the spinal column, it encloses the spinal cord and the beginnings of spinal nerves.

Both regions are lined by protective membranes called **meninges**, which shield delicate neural tissue from friction and infection.

headings.title: Ventral Body Cavity and Thoracic Subdivision
headings.content: The **ventral body cavity** is the larger anterior cavity of the human body. It is partitioned by the dome-shaped **diaphragm** into an upper thoracic cavity and a lower abdominopelvic cavity. The **thoracic cavity** itself is subdivided further into smaller compartments: the left and right **pleural cavities** (surrounding the lungs), the **pericardial cavity** (enclosing the heart), and the central **mediastinum**, which houses the heart, major blood vessels, trachea, and esophagus. This strategic arrangement allows the rhythmic movements of respiration and circulation without mechanical interference between organs.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Cavity: Regions and Quadrants
headings.content:
The **abdominopelvic cavity** is a continuous, unpartitioned space stretching from the diaphragm down to the floor of the pelvis. Although continuous, clinicians divide it into smaller geographical zones to accurately pinpoint organ pain and pathology. 

- **Four Quadrants**: Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ), Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ), Right Lower Quadrant (RLQ), and Left Lower Quadrant (LLQ). This system is vital for rapid clinical documentation during abdominal assessments.
- **Nine Regions**: Divided by two vertical and two horizontal imaginary lines into the right hypochondriac, epigastric, left hypochondriac, right lumbar, umbilical, left lumbar, right iliac, hypogastric, and left iliac regions.

headings.title: Serous Membranes and Their Functions
headings.content: Ventral body cavities and their contained organs are lined by slippery, double-layered **serous membranes** (serosa). The layer adhering directly to the organ is the **visceral layer**, while the layer lining the cavity wall is the **parietal layer**. Between these two layers lies a microscopic, fluid-filled potential space. The serous fluid secreted here drastically reduces friction generated by contracting muscles, expanding lungs, and beating hearts. Key examples include the pleura around the lungs, the pericardium around the heart, and the peritoneum within the abdominopelvic cavity.

headings.title: Clinical Significance in Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Mastering body cavity topography is essential for safe nursing practice. When a patient presents with generalized abdominal discomfort, knowing that the gallbladder resides in the right upper quadrant or that the sigmoid colon sits in the left lower quadrant guides targeted palpation and auscultation. Furthermore, pathological fluid accumulation within these cavities—such as pleural effusion in the pleural cavity or ascites in the peritoneal cavity—directly compromises vital organ function, requiring nurses to monitor respiratory rates, abdominal girth, and hemodynamic stability closely.
